passages.happening:
“Jacob also went on his way, and the angels of God met him” (verse 1).

“When Jacob saw them, he said, ‘This is the camp of God.’ So he named that place Mahanaim” (verse 2).
passages.hearers:
Two short verses, and a quiet comfort. When Jacob fled from home, he saw angels going up and down at Bethel (28:12). Now, coming home, angels meet him again. The road out and the road back are both marked by God's messengers.

Mahanaim means ‘two camps’. There is Jacob's camp, and there is God's camp. Jacob is about to be terrified of his brother's army. Before he hears of it, God shows him another army, already there.

The words ‘two camps’ will come back in this chapter. Jacob will split his people into two camps out of fear (verse 7). Then he will thank God that he, who crossed the Jordan with only a staff, has become ‘two camps’ (verse 10).

Mahanaim lay east of the Jordan and later became a real town in Israel's history. David fled there when his son Absalom rebelled against him (2 Samuel 17:24).
passages.later:
When the prophet Elisha's servant was afraid of an enemy army, Elisha prayed that his eyes would be opened, and he saw the hills full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:15-17).

A psalm says, “The angel of the LORD encamps around those who fear Him, and he delivers them” (Psalm 34:7). Hebrews calls angels “ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation” (Hebrews 1:14).
passages.asks: Before Jacob saw the danger, God showed him his camp. Ask what you fear is coming toward you. Then ask whether you have noticed the help that may already be around you.

passages.t: Esau is coming, with four hundred men
passages.happening:
Jacob sends messengers ahead to Esau in Seir, in Edom (verse 3). They are to say, “Your servant Jacob says: I have been staying with Laban and have remained there until now” (verse 4). He tells of his flocks and servants, and says he has sent word “so that I may find favor in your sight” (verse 5).

The messengers come back. “We went to your brother Esau, and now he is coming to meet you” (verse 6). Four hundred men are with him.

“In great fear and distress, Jacob divided his people into two camps, as well as the flocks and herds and camels” (verse 7). He thinks, “If Esau comes and attacks one camp, then the other camp can escape” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Twenty years ago Esau said he would kill Jacob (27:41). Jacob has not seen him since. He has no idea what Esau feels now.

Listen to his message. He calls Esau ‘my master’ and himself ‘your servant’. The stolen blessing said, ‘May you be the master of your brothers’ (27:29). Now Jacob is handing the title back. He is speaking as a servant to a king.

Seir is the rugged hill country south and east of the Dead Sea. Esau's people, the Edomites, will live there.

Four hundred men is a small army. The messengers do not say what Esau intends. Jacob assumes the worst. He is ‘in great fear and distress’, and he does what a careful man does: he makes a plan. If one camp is attacked, the other may get away.
passages.later:
Four hundred men is the size of the band David led in his years on the run (1 Samuel 22:2). Jacob had good reason to be afraid.

Israel's later history with Edom was bitter. When Israel came out of Egypt, Edom refused to let them pass through its land (Numbers 20:14-21).
passages.asks: Jacob did not know what his brother felt, so he imagined the worst. Ask whom you have avoided for years because you fear what they think of you. Then ask whether you really know, or whether you are guessing.

passages.happening:
Then Jacob prays. “O God of my father Abraham, God of my father Isaac, the LORD who told me, ‘Go back to your country and to your kindred, and I will make you prosper’” (verse 9).

“I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant. Indeed, with only my staff I came across the Jordan, but now I have become two camps” (verse 10).

“Please deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau, for I am afraid that he may come and attack me and the mothers and children with me” (verse 11).

“But You have said, ‘I will surely make you prosper, and I will make your offspring like the sand of the sea, too numerous to count’” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This is the first time Genesis shows Jacob praying for help. It is worth slowing down for.

He begins with who God is: the God of Abraham and Isaac, and the LORD who told him to go back. He stands on God's word, not on his own deserving.

Then he confesses: ‘I am unworthy.’ The man who grabbed and bargained says that everything he has is God's kindness. ‘Kindness and faithfulness’ translate two great Hebrew words for God's loyal love and his trustworthiness. They are often found together in the Bible.

Then he asks plainly: ‘Please deliver me.’ He admits he is afraid. He names the mothers and children, the people he loves.

And he ends where he began, with God's promise. ‘But You have said.’ He holds God to his own word. That is not arrogance. It is faith.

Notice what Jacob does next, though. He prays, and then he plans a gift to win Esau over. Many readers see both in him: real prayer, and the old habit of managing things himself.
passages.later:
The same pair of words, kindness and faithfulness, is how God describes himself to Moses: “abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6).

Paul writes, “Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God” (Philippians 4:6). A psalm says, “I sought the LORD, and He answered me; He delivered me from all my fears” (Psalm 34:4).
passages.asks: Jacob prayed with fear, honesty and God's promise in his hands. Ask what you are afraid of today. Then pray as he did: tell God who he is, admit what you do not deserve, ask plainly, and hold him to what he has said.

passages.happening:
Jacob spends the night there and chooses a gift for Esau: “200 female goats, 20 male goats, 200 ewes, 20 rams, 30 milk camels with their young, 40 cows, 10 bulls, 20 female donkeys, and 10 male donkeys” (verses 14-15).

He sends them ahead in separate herds, with space between each (verse 16). Each servant is to say, “They belong to your servant Jacob. They are a gift, sent to my lord Esau. And behold, Jacob is behind us” (verse 18).

“For he thought, ‘I will appease Esau with the gift that is going before me. After that I can face him, and perhaps he will accept me’” (verse 20). The gifts go ahead, and Jacob spends the night in the camp (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Five hundred and fifty animals. This is a gift fit for a king. And Jacob sends it in waves, herd after herd, with gaps between them, so that Esau meets one gift, then another, then another.

The word for ‘gift’ is the same word later used for offerings brought to God. In that world a gift was a known way to turn away someone's anger. Proverbs says, ‘A gift in secret soothes anger’ (21:14).

Verse 20 is full of the Hebrew word for ‘face’. Literally Jacob says: I will cover his face with the gift that goes before my face, and afterward I will see his face, and perhaps he will lift up my face. ‘Appease’ translates a verb that means to cover, the same verb later used for making atonement.

Jacob is trying to cover what he did twenty years ago. He has prayed. Now he is still trying to manage the outcome. But before he sees his brother's face, he will see someone else's.
passages.later:
In the next chapter Jacob presses the gift on Esau with words that echo this night: “I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God” (Genesis 33:10).

Jesus taught, “if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar. First go and be reconciled to your brother” (Matthew 5:23-24).
passages.asks: Jacob sent gifts ahead to cover an old wrong. Ask whether you are trying to make up for something by giving, instead of facing it. Then ask what it would mean to go yourself.

passages.happening:
In the night Jacob takes his two wives, the two servant women and his eleven sons, and sends them across the ford of the Jabbok, with everything he has (verses 22-23).

“So Jacob was left all alone, and there a man wrestled with him until daybreak” (verse 24).

The man cannot overpower Jacob, so he strikes the socket of Jacob's hip and puts it out of joint (verse 25). “Let me go, for it is daybreak,” the man says. “I will not let you go unless you bless me,” Jacob answers (verse 26).

“What is your name?” “Jacob” (verse 27).

“Your name will no longer be Jacob, but Israel, because you have struggled with God and with men, and you have prevailed” (verse 28).

Jacob asks, “Please tell me your name.” The man replies, “Why do you ask my name?” Then he blesses Jacob there (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The Jabbok is a river that cuts a deep valley through the hills east of the Jordan and runs down into it. A ford is a shallow place where people can wade across. In Hebrew the sounds play together: Jacob (Yaakov) wrestles (yeaveq) at the Jabbok (Yabboq).

Jacob is ‘left all alone’. Everyone he loves is on the other side. Everything he owns is gone ahead. There is no one to send, no plan to work, no gift to hide behind.

And a man wrestles with him all night. The text gives no warning and no description. We are not told where he came from.

Then the strange turn. The man ‘could not overpower Jacob’, yet with one touch he puts Jacob's hip out of joint. This was never a contest of equal strength. Whoever this is could have ended it at any time.

Jacob, hurt and unable to win, does the one thing left. He holds on. ‘I will not let you go unless you bless me.’ The man who once took a blessing by disguise now asks for one with his own arms, and gives his own name.

That is the point of the question ‘What is your name?’ The last time Jacob was asked who he was, by his blind father, he said ‘I am Esau’ (27:19, 24). Now he says, ‘Jacob’: the heel-grabber, the cheat. He tells the truth about himself. And he is given a new name.

In that world, to give someone a new name was an act of authority. The man renames Jacob, and will not give his own name. He keeps it hidden.
passages.later:
Hosea, centuries later, remembers the night: “In the womb he grasped his brother’s heel, and in his vigor he wrestled with God” (Hosea 12:3). “Yes, he struggled with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought His favor; he found Him at Bethel and spoke with Him there” (Hosea 12:4).

God confirms the new name at Bethel: “Though your name is Jacob, you will no longer be called Jacob. Instead, your name will be Israel” (Genesis 35:10).

When Samson's father later asks the angel of the LORD his name, the angel answers in almost the same words, “Why do you ask my name,” and says it is “beyond comprehension” (Judges 13:18).
passages.hard:
Who was the man? The text calls him ‘a man’ (verse 24). Jacob says afterward that he has seen God face to face (verse 30). Hosea calls him ‘the angel’ and also says Jacob ‘wrestled with God’ (Hosea 12:3-4). Readers have taken this in several ways, each as a reading.

Many Jewish readers have taken him to be an angel. One well-known tradition in Genesis Rabbah, an early Jewish commentary on Genesis, says he was the guardian angel of Esau, and the medieval Jewish teacher Rashi repeats it.

Others take the text at its word that Jacob met God himself, in a form a man could grasp, as God met Abraham at Mamre (chapter 18).

Many Christians, from the early church onward, have read the man as the Son of God appearing before he was born as a man. Justin Martyr, writing in the second century in his Dialogue with Trypho, read the scene this way. Other Christians follow Hosea and see an angel acting with God's authority.

Some modern scholars think the story grew from an older tale of a spirit guarding a river crossing; others find that reading foreign to the text. The text itself is deliberately veiled, and the man will not give his name. These notes take no side among these readings.

What does the name Israel mean? Genesis explains it by a play on sound: ‘you have struggled with God’. The Hebrew verb sounds like the name. Many scholars think the name itself may first have meant ‘God strives’ or ‘God rules’. The root is not certain. The explanation in Genesis gives the meaning the name was to carry for Jacob and his people: one who struggled with God and with men, and prevailed by holding on.

The name Israel here belongs first to one man, and then, in the Bible, to the people who came from his twelve sons. These notes make no claim about any modern state, border or conflict, as the note on Genesis 12 also says.
passages.asks: Jacob was asked his name, and for once he told the truth about himself. Ask what name you would have to give if God asked you who you really are. Then ask whether you would hold on to him, wounded, until he blessed you.

passages.t: ‘I have seen God face to face’
passages.happening:
Jacob names the place Peniel, saying, “Indeed, I have seen God face to face, and yet my life was spared” (verse 30).

“The sun rose above him as he passed by Penuel, and he was limping because of his hip” (verse 31).

“Therefore to this day the Israelites do not eat the tendon which is at the socket of the hip, because the socket of Jacob’s hip was struck near that tendon” (verse 32).
passages.hearers:
Peniel means ‘face of God’. Penuel is another form of the same name.

‘My life was spared.’ The Bible says no one can see God's face and live (Exodus 33:20). Jacob is amazed that he is alive. He has been as close to God as a man can come, and God let him go on living, and blessed him.

The sun rises. Twenty years ago the sun set as Jacob left the land at Bethel (28:11). Now it rises on him as he comes back. He is a new man with a new name.

And he is limping. He will limp for the rest of his life. Many readers find this the most important detail in the chapter. Jacob got his blessing, but he did not get it by his own strength. He walks into the land, and toward his brother, leaning on a hurt hip. He can never again forget that the blessing came from God.

The last verse explains a custom. Israel remembered this night at every meal. Jewish law still forbids eating the tendon near the hip joint of an animal, usually identified with the sciatic nerve. It must be carefully cut out, and in many places the back part of the animal is simply not eaten.
passages.later:
John writes, “No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known” (John 1:18). Paul speaks of “the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

Paul also learned that weakness can be where God's strength is seen: “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Israel's later law forbade God's people to forget what he had done for them (Deuteronomy 4:9).
passages.asks: Jacob left with a blessing and a limp. Ask whether there is a weakness in your life that has kept you leaning on God. Then ask whether you can thank him for it, as one of the ways he has blessed you.
